text: Hippo who ate hat under round-the-clock medical watch at US zoo. # Fiona the hippo on 24hr medical watch after eating hat at Cincinnati Zoo ## In short: A beloved hippo at Cincinnati Zoo has been undergoing medical treatment after swallowing a hat. The knitted cap was accidentally tossed into her enclosure by a visitor. ## What's next? Surgery has been ruled out, with zoo officials hoping the hat will pass through her system. Fiona the hippo captivated hearts around the world when she was born six weeks premature at Cincinnati Zoo in 2017. Severely underweight and unable to walk, the feeble baby had doctors from a children's hospital to thank for saving her life. Now, nine years later, she's in survival mode again. Fiona, who was named after the Shrek character, has been under 24-hour medical care for about nine days after ingesting a hat accidentally tossed into her habitat by a visitor. A child had thrown a knitted cap into the air when a ceiling fan caught and catapulted it through a small opening above the area's viewing window, Cincinnati Zoo spokesperson Michelle Curley told US media. Seemingly unharmed initially, the beloved hippo has been under constant medical supervision after staff began to notice her appetite reducing. She underwent a colonoscopy earlier in the week, but her specialist care team are hoping a new approach can help her pass the foreign object. ## Zoo hoping to shake it loose Zoo officials borrowed a vibration plate from a nearby horse farm and have encouraged Fiona to stand on it several times throughout the day. "The hope is that the vibrations will help encourage movement through her digestive tract and help the object pass," the zoo said in a statement. Surgery has been ruled out on advice from experts who said that was not an option for fully grown hippos. "Our best chance for success with Fiona would be if she could pass this on her own," zookeeper Mike Wenninger said. Fiona is now being monitored around the clock as staff employ whatever measures they can to help her pass the hat, including keeping her hydrated, giving her pain meds and feeding her her favourite foods. "Her care team even offered her a sniff of coffee, a scent she has always liked," the zoo said. "And they were happy to see her respond." An ultrasound performed on Wednesday, local time, has zoo staff optimistic the hat was beginning to pass through Fiona's small intestine. Dr Wenninger said she was "large enough that a smallish hat should be passing through". "At this point what we can do is supportive care … support her through passing it," he said. "She's getting 24-hour care and attention and we will regroup tomorrow to see how things are going, and may need another procedure in the future." The zoo said staff were rooting for Fiona and hoped she would be as "strong and resilient as she was at the beginning of her life". When she was born, Fiona weighed 13 kilograms and became the smallest hippo known to survive premature birth. Birth weights at the time ranged between 25 and 54kg for the popular zoo species, which can grow to become extremely aggressive. A Washington man wrote in The Guardian how he was disembowelled by a hippo protecting her young while on a honeymoon safari in Africa last year. Life has been far more peaceful for Fiona. Her first steps in front of cameras, nearly two weeks after birth, took social media by storm, effectively establishing her celebrity status. She earned her name due to her ears' resemblance to those of Princess Fiona from Shrek. Just eight months earlier, Cincinnati Zoo stole global headlines for entirely different reasons when the 17-year-old gorilla named Harambe was fatally shot by zoo officials after dragging a three-year-old boy who had climbed into his enclosure. **ABC/AP**
